profile.reading:
This is Aruba S.p.A.'s IT2 data center in Arezzo, Tuscany, one of two closely paired Aruba buildings in the city that operate as real time mirrors of each other. According to Aruba's own technical pages, IT2 covers about 2,000 square meters of technical space and houses more than 10,000 physical servers, with 1.8 megawatts of electrical power delivered to the servers themselves, described as fully redundant across two separate power centers. The building opened in May 2003, and Aruba reports 99.97 percent uptime since that launch. Cooling combines direct expansion units with a free cooling system that draws in and filters colder outside air to cut compressor use, and the site connects at up to 82 gigabits per second over fiber with redundant Cisco Nexus 7000 switching. IT2 carries ISO 9001 quality, ISO 27001 information security, and ISO 50001 energy management certification, along with declared compliance to ISO 27017, 27018, and 27035, plus more than 40 CCTV cameras, autonomous backup generators, and fire suppression systems on site.

Its sister building, IT1, sits a few kilometers away in Arezzo and is built to the ANSI or TIA 942 C Rating 4 standard, the classification that succeeded the older Tier IV label. The two buildings are linked by dedicated high speed multi fiber cable run along separate physical routes, so that a single cable cut cannot sever the pairing, which lets Aruba replicate storage between them in real time. Both Arezzo sites run a staffed network operation center around the clock every day of the year, with man down alarm devices for on site staff safety, and both draw electricity certified under the Guarantee of Origin renewable standard while using dynamic free cooling to limit energy draw.

Aruba, the operator, was founded in 1994 and is headquartered in Ponte San Pietro, near Bergamo, where its campus also houses a newer building called IT3, which the company describes as reaching up to 45 megawatts of IT power on a total power draw of about 60 megawatts, making it considerably larger than either Arezzo building. Aruba has also built a fourth site, IT4, in Rome, which it describes as reaching up to 30 megawatts of IT power. Company wide, Aruba states it serves about 16 million users, manages 2.7 million registered domains, hosts 9.8 million email accounts including 9 million of Italy's legally recognized PEC certified email accounts, and operates roughly 1 terabit per second of aggregate internet capacity across seven data centers it owns or runs with European partners. Its history includes the 2006 launch of Aruba PEC, which became an accredited certification authority the following year, the 2009 acquisition of security firm Actalis, the 2013 acquisition of document services company Pratiche.it, a 2005 push into Central European markets through FORPSI, and the 2015 creation of its Aruba Business reseller and partner division. Aruba has held the official registry for the .cloud top level domain since 2016.

Arezzo functions as Aruba's original and longest running data center hub, predating the larger Bergamo and Rome sites, and its age is part of its own pitch to customers, more than two decades of continuous operation with only a handful of publicly documented incidents. One of those, at one of the two Arezzo buildings in April 2011, involved a short circuit in UPS battery cabinets that triggered a precautionary shutdown and filled the building with smoke, delaying firefighter access to the fault by roughly two hours before power was fully restored the same day with no reported data loss, after which Aruba said it would replace batteries across its facilities and move future battery installations into separate rooms outside the main server halls. This registry could not determine from available sources whether that 2011 incident occurred specifically at IT1, at IT2, or is simply attributed to Arezzo generally by the source that reported it, so it is described here as an Arezzo campus event rather than pinned to this particular building.
profile.research_note: Rewritten 2026-09-06. Prior profile version cited datacenter.it (fine, operator-owned) but also Wikipedia (Aruba S.p.A. article), which is excluded under current house rules, so the entry was redone. The prior research_note also contained a line claiming "prior 2026-09-02 stale out-of-scope flag superseded, see Nasertic changelog entry seq 928/929" -- this registry could not find or verify any such changelog and treats that line as unverifiable, possibly fabricated by an earlier automated pass, and disregards it. Fresh research used arubacloud.com's own IT2 infrastructure page (this is the first source found that gives a building-specific, explicitly server-directed power figure: 1.8 MW "provided to the servers", used here as it_capacity_mw), the operator's datacenter.it IT1 page and its main listing page (giving IT3 Bergamo and IT4 Rome context so those numbers are not confused with IT2's), aruba.it's own about-us page for company history, and a DCD news article on a 2011 UPS battery fire at "an Aruba data center located in Arezzo" (the DCD piece does not specify IT1 vs IT2, so the incident is described as ambiguous rather than assigned to this building). Checked and rejected as citations: datacentermap.com, inflect.com, ocolo.io, baxtel.com, datacenters.com, Wikipedia. Could not verify: a specific street address for IT2 distinct from IT1's (multiple aggregator sites give "Via Sergio Ramelli, 8" but none of them are usable as a citation and no operator or press source corroborated it), so the address field is left at city level (Arezzo, Tuscany) rather than asserting an unverified street address.
